title: Root: sub- (under, from below)
core: Every word here puts one thing *under* another — but "under" does different work in each. In one it means beneath in rank; in another, back down to a lower level; in another, filed under a bigger heading; in the last, attacking from underneath. What makes them confusable is that all four describe a loss of height, standing, or independence, so under time pressure the prefix feels like the meaning. The discriminators are **who is doing it** and **what happens to the smaller thing**.

words.nuance: The only adjective, and the only one describing a *stance* rather than an event — a permanent posture of being under someone. It is also the only one that judges: **subservient** is a sneer, where the others are neutral reports of what occurred.

The only word with no agent at all. Nobody subsides a flood; the flood **subsides** on its own, and only because it had risen first. Where the others need someone to do them to something, this one is what a thing does when everyone stops touching it.

The smaller thing survives intact — it just loses its own heading and now counts as an instance of the bigger one. Cool and clerical: a ministry **subsumes** a department the way a category swallows an example, with no hostility and nothing damaged.

Here the "under" is where the *attacker* stands, not where the victim lands — the direction of the prefix flips. The only aggressive word in the set, and the only one that can be praise: **subverting** a genre is a compliment, **subverting** an election is a charge.

exam_note: Sentence-completion items hinge on agency — a blank whose subject acts alone (fever, uproar, swelling) can only be **subside**; if an actor is named, ask whether the smaller thing is filed (**subsume**) or hollowed out (**subvert**).
